en.title: Insurance: the whole course
en.short: What an insurance degree, diploma or professional course covers, and how to study it well.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text:
Insurance is a way to transfer risk. A person or business pays a premium, the price of cover, to an insurer. The insurer promises to pay an agreed sum or meet a loss if a defined event happens. The insurer pools many similar risks, so the losses of the few are shared across the many. This is why insurance needs probability, statistics and financial mathematics.

Insurance is also a legal and regulated business. The contract sets out what is covered, what is excluded and what the insured must disclose. Rules on insurable interest, indemnity and claims handling differ between countries. Insurance is not gambling: the insured must usually have a real interest in the thing insured, and the aim is to restore a loss, not to profit from it.

The subject therefore combines risk, law, economics, accounting, sales, ethics and actuarial science. It prepares students for work in insurers, brokers, agencies, regulators, banks and risk departments.

sections.heading: How study is usually organised
sections.text:
Length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. A bachelor’s degree in insurance commonly takes three to five years. In Nigeria, universities offer BSc Insurance and polytechnics offer ND and HND Insurance; a full-time BSc is often four years, but confirm this with the school. Professional study is separate. The Chartered Insurance Institute of Nigeria (CIIN) awards insurance qualifications, and some degrees give exemptions from parts of them.

In the United Kingdom, insurance and risk management are studied in degrees and through the Chartered Insurance Institute (CII); actuarial work follows the Institute and Faculty of Actuaries (IFoA). In many countries a master’s degree adds research methods and advanced risk topics. Professional bodies and regulators change their rules, so check the current syllabus and the regulator’s website.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Teaching usually starts with the foundations. You meet risk and uncertainty, the role of insurance, the principles of the insurance contract, insurance markets and institutions, probability and statistics, financial mathematics, risk management principles, legal foundations and accounting basics for insurers.

The core then applies these ideas. It covers insurance contract law, terms, warranties (promises in the contract) and claims; underwriting and rating (deciding which risks to accept and the price); claims management and settlement; life assurance and annuities; health insurance; property and fire insurance; liability insurance; motor insurance; marine and transport insurance; reinsurance (insurance bought by an insurer); insurance accounting and reporting; regulation and supervision; marketing and distribution; enterprise risk management for insurers; actuarial mathematics for life insurance; reserving for general insurance (setting money aside for future claims); insurance fraud; and professional ethics and governance.

At master’s level the course turns to advanced risk theory and ruin probability (the chance that an insurer runs out of money to pay claims), the economics of insurance and information, research methods, and catastrophe risk, climate change and insurance. The order can vary, but the logic is usually from risk and law to products, operations, reporting and then advanced analysis.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Insurance is learned by using the vocabulary. Keep a glossary and write a one-line definition for each term, such as premium (the price of cover), sum insured (the maximum the insurer will pay), deductible (the part the insured pays), indemnity (restoring the loss), subrogation (the insurer’s right to recover from a third party) and reserve (money set aside for claims). Read a real policy wording and mark the insuring clause, exclusions, conditions and claim duties.

Practise the calculations until the steps are automatic: present value, premium, claim reserve and ruin probability. State every assumption, because a mortality table, interest rate or expense loading changes the answer. For law and regulation, name the country and check the current statute or regulator guidance. Use past questions, but check which edition they follow. Study cases in groups and explain the decision to another student; teaching is the best test of understanding.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Common mistakes include:
Treating insurance as a bet, and forgetting insurable interest.
Assuming one country’s insurance law applies everywhere.
Confusing indemnity with a fixed benefit, as in many life policies.
Mixing reinsurance with co-insurance or with a broker’s role.
Using a formula without stating its assumptions.
Ignoring expenses, claims and lapses when pricing or reserving.
Memorising products but not the risks they cover.
Forgetting that regulation, tax and professional rules change.
Giving a calculation without checking whether the answer is sensible.

keyPoints: Insurance transfers risk by pooling many similar exposures, so that the losses of the few are shared across the many.
The insurance contract, insurable interest and claims rules are legal matters, and they differ between countries.
A typical course moves from risk, law, mathematics and accounting to products, operations, reporting and then advanced risk theory.
Calculations in insurance depend on stated assumptions, such as mortality, interest, expenses and claim frequency.
Ethics and fraud control are part of insurance practice, not optional extras.
Check the current syllabus, statute and regulator guidance, because rules and professional requirements change.

en.title: Risk, uncertainty and the role of insurance
en.short: Risk, uncertainty, peril, hazard, insurable risks, pooling, transfer, moral hazard and adverse selection.

sections.heading: Key definitions
sections.text: Risk is uncertainty about a loss or other outcome. In insurance it usually means the chance of financial loss. Uncertainty is doubt about what will happen, especially when the chance cannot be measured. Peril is the cause of a loss, such as fire or theft. Hazard is a condition that makes loss more likely or severe, such as faulty wiring.

sections.heading: What is insurable
sections.text: Insurable risks are usually accidental, definite and measurable in money. There must be many similar exposures, and one loss should not usually mean loss to all. The event must be legal and not deliberately caused. Pure risks, which involve only loss or no loss, are commonly insurable. Speculative risks, which offer gain as well as loss, such as trading, are normally uninsurable. Some risks are hard to insure because loss is hard to measure or the event is widespread. Special schemes, reinsurance or government may still cover them, so the boundary varies by country.

sections.heading: Pooling and transfer
sections.text: Insurance pools many similar risks. Policyholders pay premiums into a fund, which pays the few who suffer losses. Pooling does not remove risk, but it makes cost more predictable for the group. Risk transfer means exchanging an uncertain possible loss for a certain premium. Insurance exists because people and firms need protection from large losses they could not easily bear. It supports lending, trade and business activity. Example: Amina runs a bakery in Kano and insures her oven against fire. Fire is the peril; old wiring is a hazard. Her premium buys cover, and the insurer bears the fire loss if the policy terms are met.

sections.heading: Information problems
sections.text: Moral hazard is a change in behaviour after cover: the insured takes less care because the insurer bears the cost. Adverse selection is when higher-risk people are more likely to buy or buy more cover, and the insurer cannot tell them apart. Both can raise claims and premiums. Clear policy terms and careful checking of applicants help control them.

keyPoints: Risk is uncertainty about loss, while uncertainty is doubt that cannot be measured.
Peril is the cause of loss; hazard is a condition that increases its chance or severity.
Insurable risks are usually accidental, measurable, legal and pooled across many similar exposures.
Pooling makes losses more predictable, and risk transfer exchanges an uncertain loss for a premium.
Moral hazard is careless behaviour after cover; adverse selection is higher-risk buyers being more likely to insure.
Insurance exists to protect people and firms from large losses and to support trade and lending.

en.title: Principles of the insurance contract
en.short: The six principles of insurance contracts, with simple policy examples and a contribution calculation.

sections.heading: Interest and good faith
sections.text:
Insurable interest is the legal or financial interest an insured has in the subject matter. The insured must gain from its safety or lose from its damage. In many common-law countries, property insurance requires interest when the loss occurs, while life insurance requires it when the policy starts. Rules vary, so check local law.

Utmost good faith is a duty on both parties to disclose material facts and not mislead. A material fact is one that would influence a prudent insurer’s decision or premium. Remedies for breach differ by country. They may include avoiding the contract or refusing a claim.

sections.heading: Indemnity and sharing
sections.text:
Indemnity means the insurer restores the insured to the financial position before the loss, as far as money can. The insured should not profit. Life assurance and some personal accident covers are usually not contracts of indemnity.

Subrogation follows payment. The insurer takes over the insured’s right to recover from a third party, but only up to the amount paid. The insured cannot recover twice.

Contribution applies when two or more policies cover the same loss, same interest and same risk. The insured cannot recover more than the loss. Insurers may share pro rata by sums insured. Suppose Policy A covers 6,000,000 and Policy B covers 4,000,000, and the loss is 3,000,000. A pays 3,000,000 × 6 ÷ 10 = 1,800,000. B pays 3,000,000 × 4 ÷ 10 = 1,200,000. Total = 3,000,000.

sections.heading: Proximate cause
sections.text: Proximate cause is the dominant and effective cause of a loss, not simply the last event. It decides whether a peril is covered. Suppose fire damages stock and smoke ruins other stock. The proximate cause is fire, not smoke. If the policy covers fire, the smoke damage may also be covered. If it covers only smoke, the result may differ. Read the policy wording and local law.

keyPoints: Insurable interest is the legal or financial interest that supports the contract; timing rules vary by country and type.
Utmost good faith requires disclosure of material facts; remedies for breach differ by jurisdiction.
Indemnity restores the insured to the pre-loss position and prevents profit.
Subrogation lets the insurer recover from a third party after paying, up to the amount paid.
Contribution shares a loss among policies covering the same interest; pro rata by sums insured is one method.
Proximate cause is the dominant cause of loss, not simply the last event.

en.title: Insurance markets and institutions
en.short: Types of insurers, reinsurers and intermediaries, and the economic role of insurance markets.

sections.heading: Insurers and ownership
sections.text: An insurer is a company or mutual that accepts risks and promises to pay claims. Proprietary insurers are owned by shareholders and aim to earn profit for them. Mutual insurers are owned by their policyholders; surplus may be returned through lower premiums or dividends. Both forms may sell life or general insurance. The mix of proprietary, mutual and state-owned insurers differs by country, and so do the names and powers of regulators.

sections.heading: Intermediaries and reinsurers
sections.text: Intermediaries stand between buyers and insurers. An agent acts for the insurer, often selling its products under an agency agreement. A broker acts for the client, advises on cover and places it with insurers; the broker owes a duty to the client. Some insurers sell directly. A reinsurer is an insurer of insurers: it accepts part of the risk that a primary insurer has taken on. Reinsurance spreads very large or concentrated risks. Licensing rules and market names differ by country.

sections.heading: Economic role and case
sections.text: Insurance markets pool independent risks, transfer uncertainty and free capital for investment and trade. Premiums and insurer capital help allocate risk to those willing to bear it. Insurers are also large institutional investors. Consider a made-up case. Ngozi’s Lagos food-processing firm buys fire cover through a broker. The broker places 60% with a proprietary insurer and 40% with a mutual. The proprietary insurer cedes, or passes on, half of its 60% to a reinsurer. On a covered loss of ₦10 million, the proprietary insurer keeps 30% = ₦3 million, its reinsurer reimburses it for the other 30% = ₦3 million, and the mutual pays 40% = ₦4 million. Total = ₦10 million. No single balance sheet carries all the risk.

keyPoints: Proprietary insurers are owned by shareholders; mutual insurers are owned by policyholders.
An agent represents the insurer, while a broker represents the client.
A reinsurer insures insurers and spreads large or concentrated risks.
Insurance markets pool risk, reduce uncertainty and mobilise capital.
Market structure, institution names and licensing rules differ by country.

en.title: Probability and statistics for insurance
en.short: Random variables, expected value, variance, distributions, pooling, and frequency and severity in insurance.

sections.heading: Random variables
sections.text: A random variable is a numerical outcome whose value depends on chance, such as the loss on one policy. Its expected value, written E[X] or μ, is the probability-weighted average: E[X] = Σ x P(X = x) for a discrete variable. It is the long-run mean, not a forecast of one result. Variance measures spread around that mean: Var(X) = E[(X − μ)²] = E[X²] − μ². The standard deviation is √Var(X), in the same units as X.

sections.heading: Distributions and pooling
sections.text: Common distributions include the binomial, for the number of claims in a fixed number of policies; the Poisson, for counts in time or area, with mean and variance both λ; the exponential, for waiting times; the normal, symmetric and continuous; and the lognormal, positive and skewed, often used for claim sizes. The law of large numbers says that for many independent risks the average outcome tends to the expected value. Pooling many policies therefore makes the average claim more predictable, provided risks are not strongly correlated.

sections.heading: Frequency and severity
sections.text:
Frequency is the number of claims per exposure, often per policy year. Severity is the amount of one claim. If N is claim count and X is claim size, total loss is the sum of N claim amounts. When N and X are independent, expected total loss is E[N] × E[X]. Insurers use these ideas to set premiums and hold reserves.

Worked example: one policy has loss 0 with probability 0.98 and 50,000 with probability 0.02. E[L] = 0.02 × 50,000 = 1,000. E[L²] = 0.02 × 50,000² = 50,000,000. Var(L) = 50,000,000 − 1,000² = 49,000,000. The standard deviation is 7,000. For 1,000 independent such policies, expected total loss is 1,000 × 1,000 = 1,000,000.

keyPoints: Expected value is E[X] = Σ x P(X = x) for a discrete random variable.
Variance is Var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])², and standard deviation is its square root.
The Poisson distribution has mean and variance equal to λ; the binomial counts successes in fixed trials.
The law of large numbers makes average losses more predictable as independent policies increase.
Expected aggregate loss is E[N] × E[X] when claim count and claim size are independent.
Frequency is claims per exposure and severity is the amount per claim.

en.title: Financial mathematics for insurance
en.short: Simple and compound interest, present value, annuities, loans, sinking funds and premium finance.

sections.heading: Interest and value
sections.text: Interest is the price of using money. Simple interest is I = P × i × n, so FV = P(1 + i n). Compound interest adds interest to principal: FV = P(1 + i)^n and PV = FV ÷ (1 + i)^n. Here i is the rate per period as a decimal and n is the number of periods. For P = 100,000 at 10% for 3 years, simple FV = 100,000(1 + 0.10 × 3) = 130,000. Compound FV = 100,000(1.10)^3 = 133,100. Its PV is 133,100 ÷ 1.331 = 100,000.

sections.heading: Annuities
sections.text: An annuity is a series of equal payments at regular intervals. For an ordinary annuity, paid at each period end, PV = A × [1 − (1 + i)^−n] ÷ i and FV = A × [((1 + i)^n − 1) ÷ i]. An annuity due is paid at the start, so multiply by (1 + i). If A = 10,000, i = 8% and n = 5, the PV factor is 3.9927, so PV = 39,927.10. The FV factor is 5.8666, so FV = 58,666.01.

sections.heading: Loans and sinking funds
sections.text: A loan repaid by level instalments uses A = L × i ÷ [1 − (1 + i)^−n]. A sinking fund uses equal deposits to reach a target: D = S × i ÷ [(1 + i)^n − 1]. For L = 500,000 at 12% for 4 years, A = 500,000 × 0.12 ÷ [1 − (1.12)^−4] = 164,617.22. For S = 500,000 in 4 years at 12%, D = 500,000 × 0.12 ÷ [(1.12)^4 − 1] = 104,617.22. The deposits accumulate to 500,000.

sections.heading: Use in insurance
sections.text: Insurers receive premiums before claims arise, so they discount expected claim payments. A claim of 133,100 expected in 3 years has PV 100,000 at 10%. Premiums paid by instalments form an annuity. If 10,000 is paid at each year end for 5 years at 8%, PV = 39,927.10; if paid at the start, PV = 39,927.10 × 1.08 = 43,121.27. Insurers may charge for instalments because they lose investment income and take credit risk. Reserves for future claims grow with compound interest.

keyPoints: Simple interest: FV = P(1 + i n); compound interest: FV = P(1 + i)^n and PV = FV ÷ (1 + i)^n.
Ordinary annuity PV = A × [1 − (1 + i)^−n] ÷ i; annuity due PV = ordinary PV × (1 + i).
Loan instalment A = L × i ÷ [1 − (1 + i)^−n].
Sinking fund deposit D = S × i ÷ [(1 + i)^n − 1].
Discounting converts future claim amounts to present values; compound interest projects reserves forward.
Instalment premiums are annuities, so insurers consider lost investment income and credit risk.

en.title: Principles of risk management
en.short: Identifying, measuring and treating risk, and the risk management process.

sections.heading: Identifying and measuring
sections.text: Risk management is the coordinated set of activities a person or organisation uses to direct and control risk. Risk identification means finding what can happen, why, and where. Tools include checklists, inspections, incident records, flow charts and staff discussion. Measurement then estimates likelihood (how often) and impact (how much harm). A simple risk score multiplies likelihood by impact on a chosen scale. Expected loss is probability times average loss. Prioritisation ranks risks by score and by the organisation’s risk appetite, which is the amount of risk it is willing to accept.

sections.heading: Treating risks
sections.text: Risk control reduces likelihood or impact: avoid the activity, prevent losses, reduce harm, or detect problems early. Risk financing plans how to pay for losses that remain. Retention means keeping a risk and funding losses from savings or a reserve; it suits small, frequent losses. Transfer means another party bears the risk, commonly through insurance or a contract. Insurance transfers defined losses for a premium (the price of cover), but exclusions and excesses (amounts the insured pays first) leave some risk retained. Example: a Lagos bakery’s van has a 5% yearly chance of theft, and a theft would cost ₦400,000. Expected loss = 0.05 × 400,000 = ₦20,000. If insurance costs ₦35,000 with a ₦10,000 excess, expected retained cost = 35,000 + (0.05 × 10,000) = ₦35,500. The bakery may still insure because one severe loss could threaten cash flow; expected loss alone hides severity.

sections.heading: Process and ERM
sections.text: The risk management process usually runs: set objectives and context; identify risks; analyse and measure them; evaluate and prioritise; treat them; monitor and review; and communicate throughout. Enterprise risk management (ERM) applies this across the whole organisation, not in separate departments. It links risks to strategy, sees risks together rather than one by one, and considers risk appetite and culture. ERM is a set of ideas and practices, not one fixed law.

keyPoints: Risk management identifies, measures, prioritises and treats risks.
Risk score = likelihood × impact; expected loss = probability × average loss.
Risk control reduces likelihood or impact; risk financing pays for remaining losses.
Retention keeps a risk; transfer moves it to another party, often an insurer.
The process runs from context and identification to treatment, monitoring and communication.
ERM manages risks across the whole organisation and links them to strategy and risk appetite.

en.title: Legal foundations of insurance
en.short: Contract basics, sources of insurance law and how they differ by country.

sections.heading: Offer and acceptance
sections.text: Insurance begins with a proposal. The applicant makes an offer by completing a proposal form and sending it, usually with information the insurer needs. The insurer accepts by issuing a policy, a cover note (a temporary document proving cover until the policy is issued) or a clear written acceptance. A quotation is normally an invitation to treat, not an offer. Acceptance must be communicated; silence is not acceptance unless the parties agreed otherwise. The premium is the insured’s consideration. The insurer’s consideration is its promise to pay valid claims or provide cover.

sections.heading: Capacity, legality and agency
sections.text: Capacity means the legal ability to make a binding contract. A minor, a person with severe mental impairment or someone too intoxicated may lack capacity, and rules differ by country. Companies can contract through authorised officers. Legality means the contract’s purpose must be lawful; insurance for an illegal activity is generally void. Agency matters because brokers and agents deal with insurers. An agent acts for a principal, and the principal is bound by acts within the agent’s authority. A broker usually acts for the insured, while an agent may act for the insurer. The exact position depends on the appointment and local law.

sections.heading: Sources and example
sections.text: Insurance law comes from statutes, regulations, case law and general contract law. Statutes set licensing, solvency and policy rules; regulators issue regulations; courts interpret words and fill gaps. These sources differ by country, so a Nigerian student must check Nigerian statutes and cases, a Kenyan student Kenyan law, and so on. In a made-up case, Amina in Kano completes a motor proposal and pays the premium. The insurer issues a cover note. There is offer, acceptance and consideration. If Amina is 16 and local law treats her as lacking capacity, the contract may be unenforceable against her. If her agent exceeded authority, Amina may not be bound by the contract.

keyPoints: An insurance contract needs offer, acceptance, consideration, capacity and legality.
A proposal is usually the offer, and a policy or cover note can be acceptance.
The premium is the insured’s consideration, while the insurer’s promise is its consideration.
Capacity and legality rules differ by country, so check the local statute and cases.
An agent binds a principal only within the agent’s actual or apparent authority.
Insurance law comes from statute, regulation, case law and general contract law, and these vary by country.

en.title: Accounting basics for insurers
en.short: Premium income, claims, expenses, technical reserves, insurer statements and simple ratios.

sections.heading: Premium income
sections.text: Insurers record gross written premium (GWP), the premium before reinsurance is deducted. Net written premium is GWP minus reinsurance ceded. Accounts also match premium to the period of cover. Earned premium is the part of premium for risk that has expired in the accounting period. The unearned premium reserve is a liability for cover still to run. For example, a one-year policy taken out on 1 October has three months earned by 31 December, so one quarter of its premium is earned and three quarters are unearned.

sections.heading: Claims and reserves
sections.text: Claims incurred are claims paid in the period plus the change in the outstanding claims reserve. The reserve covers claims reported but not yet settled. It also includes IBNR, incurred but not reported claims. Life insurers hold mathematical reserves for future policy benefits. These reserves are technical reserves. Expenses include commissions and administration. Underwriting result equals earned premium minus claims incurred minus expenses. Investment income is shown separately.

sections.heading: Statements and ratios
sections.text: The statement of financial position lists assets such as investments, cash, reinsurance assets and receivables; liabilities such as technical reserves and payables; and equity. The statement of profit or loss shows premium, reinsurance, claims, expenses, investment income and tax. Layout varies by country and reporting framework, such as IFRS 17. Loss ratio = claims incurred ÷ earned premium. Expense ratio = expenses ÷ earned premium. Combined ratio = loss ratio + expense ratio. Below 100% means an underwriting profit.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A made-up insurer has earned premium 500,000, claims incurred 300,000 and expenses 150,000. Loss ratio = 300,000 ÷ 500,000 = 60%. Expense ratio = 150,000 ÷ 500,000 = 30%. Combined ratio = 60% + 30% = 90%. Underwriting profit = 500,000 − 300,000 − 150,000 = 50,000. Check: 10% of 500,000 = 50,000. If investment income is 20,000, profit before tax is 70,000.

keyPoints: Gross written premium is premium before reinsurance; net written premium is gross written premium minus reinsurance ceded.
Earned premium is the part of premium for cover expired in the period; unearned premium is a liability.
Claims incurred equal claims paid plus the change in outstanding claims reserves, including IBNR.
Technical reserves include unearned premium, outstanding claims and, for life insurers, mathematical reserves.
Loss ratio = claims incurred ÷ earned premium; expense ratio = expenses ÷ earned premium; combined ratio = loss ratio + expense ratio.
A combined ratio below 100% indicates an underwriting profit before investment income.

en.title: Insurance contract law: terms, warranties and claims
en.short: Policy terms, warranties, disclosure, causation, waiver and the legal handling of claims.

sections.heading: Terms and warranties
sections.text: Policy terms set out cover, exclusions and duties. A warranty is a promise that a state of affairs exists or will be kept. Under traditional common law, breach of warranty discharges the insurer, even if the breach did not cause the loss. The UK Insurance Act 2015 changed this for non-consumer contracts: cover is suspended while the breach continues. A condition precedent must be met before the insurer is liable, such as prompt notice. Breach may let the insurer refuse the claim. Check the governing law.

sections.heading: Disclosure and representations
sections.text: Before the contract, the insured must not misrepresent facts. A representation is a statement of fact that induces the contract; it must be substantially true. Insurance also imposes a duty of disclosure of material facts, often called utmost good faith. A fact is material if it would influence a prudent insurer. The UK Consumer Insurance (Disclosure and Representations) Act 2012 protects consumers, and the Insurance Act 2015 sets a duty of fair presentation for non-consumer insureds. Other countries differ.

sections.heading: Causation and claims
sections.text: Causation decides whether a loss falls within cover. The insured must show that an insured peril was the proximate cause, the dominant or effective cause. If an excluded peril is the proximate cause, the claim fails. Example: Amina insures her shop against fire but not explosion. A gas explosion damages the shop and starts a fire. If explosion is the effective cause, the fire damage may not be covered; if fire is, it may be. Claims require notice, proof and investigation. Limitation periods vary by country.

sections.heading: Waiver and estoppel
sections.text: Waiver is the voluntary giving up of a known right. Estoppel prevents a party from asserting a right after conduct led the other to believe it would not be enforced. If an insurer accepts late claim documents without reserving its rights, it may later be unable to rely on the late-notice condition. The insured must show knowledge and reliance. Insurers should state any reservation clearly.

keyPoints: A warranty is a policy promise; at traditional common law its breach discharges liability even without causation.
The UK Insurance Act 2015 suspends cover for breach of warranty in non-consumer contracts.
A condition precedent must be satisfied before the insurer is liable.
A representation must be substantially true, and material facts must be disclosed.
The insured must prove an insured peril was the proximate cause of the loss.
Waiver or estoppel can stop an insurer relying on a policy right if it led the insured to believe otherwise.

en.title: Underwriting and rating of insurance risks
en.short: How insurers select risks, set premiums and use class, experience and no-claims rating.

sections.heading: Selection and underwriting
sections.text: Underwriting is the process of deciding whether to accept a risk, on what terms and at what price. Risk selection means choosing risks that fit the insurer’s appetite and avoiding those likely to produce claims much above average. The underwriter may accept at standard terms, add an extra premium, impose an exclusion or excess, or decline. Good selection protects solvency and keeps premiums fair for similar policyholders. Rules and permitted factors differ by country, so check the local regulator.

sections.heading: Premium components
sections.text: A gross premium has parts. The risk premium, also called the pure premium, is the expected cost of claims. The expense loading covers administration, commission and acquisition. A profit and contingency margin allows for uncertainty and return. Some life premiums also reflect investment income. Rating factors are characteristics linked to expected claims, such as age, location, sum insured or claims history. They must be supported by evidence and applied within the law.

sections.heading: Class and experience
sections.text: Class rating prices a group with similar risk, for example all private cars of a type in a region. Experience rating adjusts the price for the individual’s past claims. A no-claims discount (NCD) rewards claim-free years. Suppose a made-up insurer sets a gross premium of 100,000. Risk premium is 60,000, expenses 25,000 and margin 15,000. Check: 60,000 + 25,000 + 15,000 = 100,000. A 30% NCD gives 100,000 × 0.70 = 70,000. After one claim the discount may fall, so the next premium rises.

sections.heading: Life and general
sections.text: Life underwriting focuses on mortality and morbidity. It uses age, health, family history, occupation, lifestyle and sum assured, and may require medical tests. General insurance underwriting focuses on the chance and size of insured events, such as fire, theft or liability. Motor and property ratings often use vehicle or building details, location and security. Life and general both need enough data, clear policy wording and regular review of rates.

keyPoints: Underwriting selects risks and sets terms; rating sets the price.
Gross premium = risk premium + expense loading + profit and contingency margin, though components vary.
Class rating uses group averages; experience rating and no-claims discounts adjust for individual claims history.
A 30% no-claims discount on a 100,000 premium gives 70,000.
Life underwriting assesses mortality and morbidity; general underwriting assesses event frequency and severity.
Rating factors must be evidence-based and allowed by the local regulator.

en.title: Claims management and settlement
en.short: From notification to payment: investigation, loss adjustment, indemnity, salvage, subrogation and complaints.

sections.heading: Notification and investigation
sections.text: The insured must notify the insurer promptly, usually through a claims form, and give proof of loss and cooperation. Late notice can prejudice a claim, but the effect depends on the policy and the law of the country. A loss adjuster, an independent or insurer-appointed specialist, investigates cause, date, cover and amount. Loss adjustment quantifies the loss and applies limits, exclusions, sums insured and deductibles. Investigation should be proportionate and fair, and it must separate suspicion from proof.

sections.heading: Indemnity and settlement
sections.text: Indemnity means restoring the insured to the financial position held before the loss, no better and no worse. Settlement may be cash, repair, replacement or reinstatement. Reinstatement pays the cost to rebuild or replace, subject to the sum insured and policy conditions; betterment, where the new item is worth more, may be deducted. A simple case: admitted loss 600,000, salvage value 50,000 kept by the insured, policy excess 25,000. Settlement = 600,000 − 50,000 − 25,000 = 525,000. Check the policy for average or underinsurance clauses.

sections.heading: Salvage and subrogation
sections.text: Salvage is what remains of damaged property. If the insured keeps it, its value is deducted from the claim; if the insurer pays a total loss, it may take the salvage and sell it to reduce its net cost. Subrogation is the insurer’s right, after paying, to stand in the insured’s place and recover from a third party who caused the loss. The insured must not destroy that right by settling with the third party. Recovery cannot exceed the amount paid, and the insured keeps any uninsured loss.

sections.heading: Fraud and complaints
sections.text: Fraud indicators include inconsistent dates, altered receipts, exaggerated losses, late notice, refusal to provide evidence and repeated claims. They are warning signs, not proof; investigate before accusing. Complaint handling should acknowledge the complaint, record it, investigate promptly, explain the decision and offer escalation. Many countries provide an insurance ombudsman or a regulator’s complaints unit, but names and powers vary, so check the local official source.

keyPoints: Indemnity restores the insured to the pre-loss financial position, no better and no worse.
Settlement = admitted loss − salvage retained by the insured − policy excess or deductible, subject to the sum insured.
Reinstatement pays rebuild or replacement cost, subject to policy conditions and possible betterment deductions.
Salvage reduces the claim; subrogation lets the insurer recover from a third party after payment.
Fraud indicators justify investigation, not accusation.
Complaints should be recorded, investigated promptly, explained and escalated where local rules allow.

en.title: Life assurance and annuities
en.short: Term, whole life and endowment cover, annuities, policy provisions, mortality tables and life reserves.

sections.heading: Term, whole life, endowment
sections.text: Term assurance pays an agreed sum if the life assured dies within a fixed period. If the person survives, the policy ends and usually pays nothing. Whole life assurance pays on death whenever it occurs, so it is permanent protection. Endowment assurance pays on death within the term or on survival to the maturity date. It combines protection with a savings element. Premiums are higher for whole life and endowment than for comparable term cover because payment is more certain. Product names and tax treatment differ by country, so check local rules.

sections.heading: Annuities and provisions
sections.text: An annuity converts a lump sum into regular income. A life annuity pays for as long as the annuitant lives; a temporary annuity pays for a fixed term. An immediate annuity starts payments soon, while a deferred annuity starts later. A guaranteed period ensures payments continue to a beneficiary if the annuitant dies early. Policy provisions set out premium payment, grace period, reinstatement and the beneficiary who receives the death benefit. A surrender ends the policy early in return for a cash value, if the contract has one. Term policies often have no surrender value. Nomination rules and surrender rights vary by country and contract.

sections.heading: Mortality tables and reserves
sections.text: A mortality table gives qx, the probability that a person aged x dies before age x+1. It also shows lx, the number alive at age x, and dx, the number dying. Insurers use these probabilities with interest to value benefits. A life reserve is the amount the insurer should hold for future obligations. In a simple net premium reserve, reserve = present value of future benefits − present value of future net premiums. Example: a one-year term policy pays 1,000,000 at year end if a 40-year-old dies. Suppose q40 = 0.002 and interest is 5%. Expected present value = 1,000,000 × 0.002 ÷ 1.05 = 1,904.76. That is the single premium before expenses and profit.

keyPoints: Term assurance pays only if death occurs within the term, while whole life assurance pays whenever death occurs.
Endowment assurance pays at death within the term or at maturity if the life survives.
A life annuity provides income for life; a temporary annuity lasts only for a fixed term.
A surrender ends cover early and may return a cash value, but term policies often have none.
A mortality table gives qx, the probability of death before the next birthday, and lx, the number alive at age x.
Net premium reserve = present value of future benefits − present value of future net premiums.

en.title: Health insurance and medical expense cover
en.short: Indemnity and managed care, benefit design, rating, moral hazard, claims control and regulation.

sections.heading: Models of cover
sections.text: Health insurance pays for medical expenses. In the indemnity model, the insurer reimburses the actual cost of covered care up to a limit. The insured usually pays a deductible, the amount paid before the insurer pays, and co-insurance, a share of the remaining bill. In managed care, the insurer contracts a provider network and controls use through gatekeeping, where a primary doctor controls referrals, and pre-authorisation, approval before treatment. Capitation pays a provider a fixed amount per member per period, so the provider shares cost risk. Systems differ by country: the United Kingdom’s NHS is tax funded, Germany’s statutory health insurance is social insurance, and Nigeria has a national health insurance authority.

sections.heading: Benefit design
sections.text: Benefit design sets covered services, such as hospital care and drugs, and the exclusions. It sets limits, waiting periods, deductibles, co-payments (fixed visit charges), and rules on pre-existing conditions. Good design balances access, cost and adverse selection, the tendency of sicker people to buy or keep cover. Moral hazard is the tendency to use more care because insurance lowers the price at the point of use. Providers may create demand. Cost sharing reduces moral hazard but can discourage necessary care, so essential services are often protected.

sections.heading: Rating and claims
sections.text:
Community rating charges the same premium to all members of a pool. It spreads risk, but healthy members may leave if premiums rise, causing adverse selection. Experience rating sets a group’s premium from its own past claims plus expenses and a margin. It rewards good claims but can penalise sick groups. Claims control includes pre-authorisation, case management, audits, provider networks and fraud detection. Regulation usually covers licensing, solvency, reserves, consumer protection, mandated benefits and rate review, but rules depend on the country.

Worked example: an eligible bill is 120,000. The deductible is 20,000 and co-insurance is 20%. The insurer pays (120,000 − 20,000) × 80% = 80,000. The patient pays 20,000 + 20,000 = 40,000. Check: 80,000 + 40,000 = 120,000.

keyPoints: Indemnity cover reimburses actual medical costs up to a limit, subject to deductibles and co-insurance.
Managed care controls cost and use through provider networks, gatekeeping, pre-authorisation and capitation.
Benefit design balances access, cost, adverse selection and moral hazard.
Community rating spreads risk across a pool; experience rating uses a group’s own claims.
Insurer payment = (eligible cost − deductible) × insurer share, subject to policy limits.
Health insurance systems, mandated benefits and regulation differ by country.

en.title: Property, fire and business interruption insurance
en.short: Fire, burglary, all risks and business interruption, with indemnity, average and claims.

sections.heading: Covers
sections.text: Fire insurance covers damage to buildings, contents or stock by fire, lightning and often explosion or smoke, as listed in the policy. Burglary insurance covers loss of property by theft involving forcible and violent entry to or exit from the premises, and damage caused during the theft. Property all risks cover is wider: it pays for accidental loss or damage unless the policy excludes it. Business interruption insurance pays lost profit and extra working costs after insured property damage, during an agreed indemnity period.

sections.heading: Indemnity and reinstatement
sections.text: Indemnity restores the insured to the financial position before the loss, so payment is based on the value of the damaged property at the time of loss, allowing for wear and tear. Reinstatement cover pays the cost of rebuilding or replacing with new property of similar type and quality, up to the sum insured. It can leave the insured better off, so policies may reduce payment for the improvement in value or require the sum insured to reflect full reinstatement cost.

sections.heading: Average and coinsurance
sections.text: An average clause reduces a claim when the sum insured is less than the value at risk. The formula is claim = loss × sum insured ÷ value at risk. A coinsurance clause requires the sum insured to be at least a stated percentage of value, such as 80%, and applies a similar reduction if it is not. Example: a building worth 500,000 is insured for 300,000. Fire causes loss of 100,000. Claim = 100,000 × 300,000 ÷ 500,000 = 60,000. The insured bears 40,000.

sections.heading: Underwriting and claims
sections.text: Underwriters assess construction, occupancy, protection, housekeeping, claims history and catastrophe exposure. They set terms, deductibles and sums insured, and check that values are adequate. On a claim, the insurer is notified promptly; the insured mitigates damage and proves the loss. A loss adjuster investigates, salvage (the damaged remains) is sold, and the insurer may recover money from a negligent third party through subrogation. Fraud is a ground for refusing the claim.

keyPoints: Fire and burglary policies cover named perils, while property all risks covers accidental loss except exclusions.
Business interruption pays lost profit and extra costs after insured property damage, within the indemnity period.
Indemnity pays the old for old value; reinstatement pays new for old, the cost of rebuilding or replacing.
Average claim = loss × sum insured ÷ value at risk.
A coinsurance clause requires the sum insured to reach a stated percentage of value.
Underwriters rate construction, occupancy, protection and claims history; claims need prompt notice, mitigation and proof.

en.title: Liability insurance
en.short: Public, product and employers’ liability, negligence, limits and claims-made cover.

sections.heading: Three liability covers
sections.text: Public liability covers claims by third parties for bodily injury or property damage arising from the insured’s premises or operations. Product liability covers harm caused by goods the insured supplied. Employers’ liability covers employees injured at work. In many countries employers’ liability insurance is compulsory, but the rules differ, so check the local statute. These policies pay damages the insured is legally liable for, plus defence costs. They do not cover the insured’s own injury or property.

sections.heading: Negligence and liability
sections.text: Legal liability usually rests on negligence: a duty of care, breach of that duty, causation and loss. Some countries also impose strict liability for defective products, so fault need not be proved. Insurance cannot cover deliberate wrongdoing or criminal fines. The insurer normally defends the claim and pays up to the policy limit.

sections.heading: Limits and triggers
sections.text:
A limit is the most the insurer pays, either per claim or in total for the policy period. A deductible, also called an excess, is the first amount the insured pays. Occurrence cover responds if the injury or damage happened during the policy period, even if the claim arrives later. Claims-made cover responds if the claim is made and reported during the period, which suits professional risks.

Example: a policy has a 5,000,000 limit and a 100,000 deductible. Damages are 1,200,000 and defence costs 300,000. Total outlay is 1,500,000. The insurer pays 1,500,000 − 100,000 = 1,400,000, within the limit. Check whether defence costs are inside or outside the limit.

sections.heading: Underwriting and claims
sections.text: Underwriters assess activities, contracts, safety records, claims history and territory. Liability is often long-tail: claims may arrive years after the policy ends, so reserves and claims-made terms matter. Claims staff check notification, liability, policy wording and possible recoveries.

keyPoints: Public, product and employers’ liability protect against third-party and employee claims.
Negligence requires duty, breach, causation and loss.
Occurrence cover follows when the injury happened; claims-made cover follows when the claim is made.
A limit caps payment; a deductible is the insured’s first share.
Long-tail liability needs careful reserving and claims handling.

en.title: Motor insurance: cover, rating and claims
en.short: Compulsory third-party cover, own damage, theft and fire, rating, no-claims discounts, exclusions and claims.

sections.heading: Cover and law
sections.text: Motor insurance protects against losses involving a vehicle. Compulsory third-party cover is the minimum required in many countries. It pays for injury or death caused to other people, and sometimes damage to their property, but not damage to the insured vehicle. The exact law, minimum limits and penalties differ by country, so check the local regulator. Own damage cover is optional and pays for accidental damage to the insured car. Theft and fire cover may be included with own damage or bought separately. A comprehensive policy usually combines third-party liability, own damage, theft and fire, but the definition varies.

sections.heading: Rating and discounts
sections.text: Insurers rate motor risks using factors linked to expected claims. These include vehicle group, engine size, repair cost, driver age and experience, claims history, where the car is kept, annual mileage and use such as private or business. An excess is the first part of a claim the policyholder pays. A no-claims discount (NCD) reduces the premium after claim-free years. It is usually stepped, for example 20%, 30% and so on, and a claim can reduce or remove it. NCD rules vary by insurer.

sections.heading: Exclusions and claims
sections.text: Policies exclude certain losses. Common examples are driving without a valid licence, driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs, racing, using the car outside the described use, intentional damage, wear and tear, and undeclared modifications. After a loss, notify the insurer promptly and report to the police where required. Provide documents and allow an assessor to inspect. The insurer may repair, pay a cash amount or write off the vehicle. The excess is deducted from the settlement.

sections.heading: Illustrative example
sections.text: Made-up figures only. Base premium is 100,000. The driver earns a 20% NCD. Net premium = 100,000 × (1 − 0.20) = 80,000. An own damage repair costs 80,000 and the excess is 25,000. Insurer payment = 80,000 − 25,000 = 55,000. The policyholder pays 25,000. A claim may also cut the next renewal discount.

keyPoints: Compulsory third-party cover protects other people, not the insured vehicle, and the law varies by country.
Own damage, theft and fire cover are usually optional and may be combined in a comprehensive policy.
Rating factors include vehicle group, driver age and experience, claims history, location and use.
A no-claims discount reduces the premium after claim-free years but can be lost after a claim.
Common exclusions include unlicensed driving, alcohol or drugs, racing, undeclared modifications and wear and tear.
With illustrative figures, net premium = base premium × (1 − NCD), and insurer payment = assessed loss − excess.

en.title: Marine and transport insurance
en.short: Hull, cargo and freight cover, sea perils, averages, salvage and transport risk.

sections.heading: Three marine covers
sections.text: Marine insurance protects ships and goods in transit. Hull insurance covers the ship itself and may include collision liability. Cargo insurance covers goods carried. Freight insurance covers the shipowner’s or carrier’s earnings if the voyage is interrupted. Cover may be for a voyage or for a period of time. Policy wording differs between markets, so read the actual clauses.

sections.heading: Perils and averages
sections.text: Perils of the sea are fortuitous accidents of navigation, such as grounding or heavy weather. They do not include ordinary wear and tear. Particular average means damage to one interest, such as one cargo owner’s goods; that owner or insurer bears it. General average is a voluntary sacrifice or expense made for the common safety. All saved interests contribute in proportion to their saved values, and an average adjuster calculates the shares.

sections.heading: Salvage and sue and labour
sections.text: Salvage is saving property at sea. A salvor may claim a reward, and salvage charges can be recoverable under a marine policy. Sue and labour expenses are costs the insured spends to avert or reduce a loss. Many policies treat these as recoverable in addition to the sum insured, but the clause wording varies.

sections.heading: Cargo clauses and example
sections.text: Cargo clauses set out insured risks, exclusions and duration. The London market’s Institute Cargo Clauses A, B and C are common; A is widest. Trade terms such as Incoterms CIF and CIP allocate insurance duties, but current versions and required cover must be checked. Made-up example: tug hire of 12,000 is spent to refloat a grounded ship for common safety. Saved values are ship 300,000 and cargo 100,000, total 400,000. Contribution rate = 12,000 ÷ 400,000 = 3%. Ship pays 300,000 × 3% = 9,000; cargo pays 100,000 × 3% = 3,000.

keyPoints: Hull covers the ship, cargo covers goods, and freight covers earnings from carriage.
Perils of the sea are fortuitous accidents, not ordinary wear and tear.
Particular average is borne by the affected interest; general average is shared by saved interests.
General average contribution = saved value × (common expense ÷ total saved value).
Salvage rewards saving property; sue and labour covers expenses to avert or reduce loss.
Cargo clauses and trade terms vary, so check the current policy and Incoterms version.

en.title: Reinsurance
en.short: Facultative and treaty cover, proportional and excess of loss, retentions, limits and retrocession.

sections.heading: Purpose and terms
sections.text: Reinsurance is insurance for insurers. The cedant buys cover from a reinsurer and cedes part of its risk and premium. The original policyholder still claims from the cedant, not the reinsurer. Reinsurance supports capacity, letting an insurer accept risks larger than its capital alone would allow. It supports solvency by capping the effect of large or clustered claims, and it can steady results. A retention is the amount the cedant keeps; a limit is the most the reinsurer will pay. Retrocession is reinsurance bought by a reinsurer.

sections.heading: Facultative and treaty
sections.text: Facultative reinsurance is arranged risk by risk. The cedant offers a risk and the reinsurer may accept or decline, so facultative cover suits unusual or very large risks. Treaty reinsurance is a standing agreement that automatically covers a defined class or portfolio under its terms. Most treaties oblige the cedant to cede all risks within scope and the reinsurer to accept them. Treaty provides automatic capacity; facultative provides selective protection.

sections.heading: Proportions, limits and example
sections.text: In proportional reinsurance the reinsurer shares premium and claims in a fixed proportion. A quota share cedes a set percentage of every risk. A surplus treaty cedes the amount above the cedant’s retention, up to a stated maximum. In non-proportional reinsurance the reinsurer pays only losses above an attachment point, up to a limit. Excess of loss cover works per risk or per event; stop loss protects the year’s loss ratio. Example: a quota share cedes 75%. A policy has premium 8,000 and a loss of 400,000. The cedant keeps 25%: premium 2,000 and loss 100,000. The reinsurer takes 6,000 premium and pays 300,000. Under excess of loss with retention 500,000 and limit 1,500,000, a 2,200,000 loss leaves the cedant paying 700,000 and the reinsurer 1,500,000.

keyPoints: Reinsurance is insurance for insurers: the cedant cedes risk and premium to a reinsurer.
Facultative is arranged risk by risk; treaty automatically covers risks within its scope.
Proportional reinsurance shares premium and claims in proportion; non-proportional pays losses above a retention up to a limit.
Cedant’s quota share recovery = ceded percentage × loss.
Excess of loss recovery = min(max(loss − retention, 0), limit).
Retrocession is reinsurance bought by a reinsurer, and reinsurance supports capacity and solvency without changing the original policyholder’s claim against the cedant.

en.title: Insurance accounting and financial reporting
en.short: Premium and claim accounting, unearned premium and claim reserves, solvency reporting and IFRS 17.

sections.heading: Premium and claims
sections.text: Insurers record premiums when policies are written, but report income as cover is provided. Gross written premium is before reinsurance; net written premium deducts reinsurance ceded. Earned premium is the part of premium for cover already given. Acquisition costs, such as commission, are expensed or deferred under the reporting framework. Claims are recorded when notified. Claims paid are cash settlements. Claims incurred include paid claims plus the change in claim reserves. A claim reserve estimates reported claims not yet settled.

sections.heading: Reserves
sections.text: Two reserves are central. The unearned premium reserve (UPR) is the unexpired part of premium, treated as a liability. The outstanding claims reserve estimates reported but unpaid claims plus claims incurred but not reported (IBNR). Example: a one-year policy written on 1 October for ₦120,000. At 31 December, 3 months are earned and 9 unearned. UPR = ₦120,000 × 9 ÷ 12 = ₦90,000. Earned premium = ₦120,000 − ₦90,000 = ₦30,000. If reported unpaid claims are ₦50,000 and IBNR is ₦10,000, the claim reserve is ₦60,000.

sections.heading: Solvency reporting
sections.text: Solvency reporting shows whether an insurer can meet obligations. It compares available capital with the capital the regulator requires. A simple ratio is available capital ÷ required capital. If assets are ₦500m and liabilities ₦420m, available capital is ₦80m. With required capital of ₦50m, the ratio is 80 ÷ 50 = 1.6, or 160%. Rules, formats and minimum ratios differ by country, so check the current local regulator’s requirements.

sections.heading: IFRS 17
sections.text: IFRS 17 Insurance Contracts is an international standard issued by the IASB. It measures contracts using fulfilment cash flows: expected cash flows, discounting and a risk adjustment, plus a contractual service margin (CSM). The CSM is unearned profit, recognised over the cover period. Revenue is reported as insurance service revenue as service is provided, not when cash is received. Contracts are grouped, and losses on onerous groups are recognised immediately. Local rules still apply; countries may adopt IFRS 17 with modifications or later dates.

keyPoints: Gross written premium is before reinsurance; net written premium deducts reinsurance ceded.
Earned premium is premium for cover already provided, and the unearned premium reserve is the unexpired part.
Claims incurred = claims paid plus the change in claim reserves, and reserves include IBNR.
Solvency ratio = available capital ÷ required capital, and local rules set the minimum.
IFRS 17 measures contracts using fulfilment cash flows plus the contractual service margin, and revenue is recognised as service is provided.
Local reporting rules differ by country and must be checked alongside IFRS 17.

en.title: Insurance regulation and supervision
en.short: Licensing, capital and solvency, market conduct, policyholder protection and supervisory tools.

sections.heading: Licensing and purpose
sections.text: Insurance supervision protects policyholders and supports market confidence. An insurer must be licensed, or authorised, before carrying on insurance business. The regulator checks ownership, management, fit and proper persons, the business plan, capital, reinsurance and systems. It may attach conditions, restrict lines of business or refuse the application. Licensing is not one-off: supervisors monitor the insurer throughout its life.

sections.heading: Capital and solvency
sections.text:
Capital absorbs losses. Solvency means an insurer can meet its liabilities as they fall due. Regulators set minimum capital and a solvency margin, often linked to risk. Assets must be admissible, meaning available and not overstated. Technical provisions are estimated liabilities to policyholders.

Illustrative example, not a real rule: liabilities 800 million, admissible assets 1,000 million, required solvency capital 150 million.
Available capital = 1,000 − 800 = 200 million.
Excess = 200 − 150 = 50 million.
Solvency ratio = 200 ÷ 150 = 133%, so the insurer passes a 100% requirement.

sections.heading: Market conduct
sections.text: Market conduct rules govern how insurers and intermediaries sell and service policies. They cover clear disclosure of cover and exclusions, fair treatment, honest advice, prompt claims handling and complaints. Policyholder protection may include a complaints scheme or ombudsman, a compensation or guarantee fund for failed insurers, and priority claims in winding up. These schemes differ by country and have limits, so read the local rules.

sections.heading: Supervisory tools
sections.text: Supervisors use off-site returns, on-site inspections, stress tests, early-warning indicators and enforcement. They may require remedial plans, restrict dividends or new business, or take control in serious cases. Regulators include the National Insurance Commission (NAICOM) in Nigeria, the Prudential Regulation Authority and Financial Conduct Authority in the United Kingdom, and the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI). In the United States, state insurance departments regulate insurers, coordinated through the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC). Rules change, so check the current official source.

keyPoints: Licensing checks fit and proper management, business plan, capital and systems before an insurer may trade.
Solvency means assets can cover liabilities and the required solvency margin.
Available capital = admissible assets − liabilities; solvency ratio = available capital ÷ required capital.
Market conduct rules require fair selling, clear disclosure, prompt claims handling and accessible complaints.
Policyholder protection can include ombudsman schemes, guarantee funds and priority claims, but limits differ by country.
Supervisors use returns, inspections, stress tests and enforcement, and rules change, so check the current official source.

en.title: Insurance marketing and distribution
en.short: Customer needs, product design, pricing communication, agents, brokers, bancassurance, digital channels and sales ethics.

sections.heading: Customer needs and design
sections.text:
Marketing starts with the customer’s need: cover for a loss too large to carry alone. Product design turns that need into a contract. The insurer sets the sum insured (maximum payout), excess (first part of each claim the customer pays), exclusions (losses not covered), term (how long cover lasts) and premium (the price). A small shop needs fire cover with realistic cover and a modest excess, not a policy full of exclusions.

Pricing communication explains the premium: the rate, sum insured, discounts, taxes and charges. If the sum insured is ₦2,000,000 and the annual rate is 0.5%, the premium is 2,000,000 × 0.005 = ₦10,000 before charges and tax.

sections.heading: Agents, brokers and banks
sections.text:
A distribution channel is the route by which a product reaches the customer. An insurance agent usually acts for the insurer and sells its products. A broker usually acts for the client, advises on needs and places cover with an insurer; legal definitions differ by country. Bancassurance is the sale of insurance through a bank, often with the bank acting as the insurer’s agent. Staff must not bundle products or imply a loan requires unnecessary cover.

Digital channels include insurer websites, apps, comparison sites and social media. They can lower costs and widen access, but must still give clear product information, record consent and allow complaints. The customer must know who acts for whom.

sections.heading: Sales ethics and disclosure
sections.text:
Ethical selling is needs-based: gather facts, recommend a suitable product and explain it plainly. Disclosure means revealing material facts (facts that would change an insurer’s decision or the premium): commission or fees, the insurer’s identity, exclusions, waiting periods and the claims process. Customers must disclose material facts truthfully; non-disclosure can affect a claim.

Mis-selling is selling an unsuitable product or hiding key facts. A bank clerk who sells an investment-linked policy to a customer wanting safe savings, without saying early surrender may lose money, has mis-sold. Cooling-off periods, commission rules and broker definitions vary by country; check the local regulator.

keyPoints: Marketing starts from customer needs and designs clear cover around them.
Premium = sum insured × rate, and communication should show charges and exclusions.
Agents usually represent insurers, while brokers usually represent clients, but legal definitions vary by country.
Bancassurance and digital channels widen access but must give clear information, record consent and allow complaints.
Ethical selling is needs-based and discloses commission, exclusions and conflicts of interest.
Mis-selling and non-disclosure can harm customers and affect claims; rules differ by country, so check the local regulator.

en.title: Enterprise risk management for insurers
en.short: Risk appetite, registers, capital, scenarios, continuity and ORSA-type assessments.

sections.heading: Framework and appetite
sections.text:
Enterprise risk management (ERM) is a firm-wide process for identifying, measuring, managing and reporting risks that affect an insurer’s objectives. These include underwriting, market, credit, liquidity, operational and strategic risks. ERM connects them rather than treating each in isolation.

Risk appetite is the amount and type of risk the board is willing to accept to pursue its objectives. It is expressed as limits, such as a maximum loss from one event or a minimum solvency ratio. A risk register lists each risk, its owner, likelihood, impact, controls and actions. It is a living tool, reviewed regularly. Risk culture, the shared attitudes and behaviour towards risk, determines whether the framework works.

sections.heading: Capital, scenarios, continuity
sections.text:
Capital absorbs unexpected losses. Solvency means assets exceed liabilities and available capital meets the required level. Eligible capital is the capital that counts towards the regulatory requirement. Scenario analysis asks what happens under plausible adverse events, while stress testing uses severe but plausible conditions. Business continuity planning keeps critical functions, such as claims handling and payments, running after disruption.

Worked example. An insurer has eligible capital of 600 million and required capital of 400 million. Solvency ratio = 600 ÷ 400 = 150%. A scenario loss of 150 million reduces capital to 450 million. The scenario ratio = 450 ÷ 400 = 112.5%. If the board’s risk appetite sets a minimum of 120%, the scenario breaches the limit. Management must then reduce risk, raise capital or buy reinsurance.

sections.heading: ERM and solvency
sections.text:
ERM supports solvency by showing how risks can erode capital and by linking risk limits to capital needs. An own risk and solvency assessment (ORSA) is the insurer’s own forward-looking view of its risks, capital needs and solvency under normal and stressed conditions. It should be owned by the board and senior management, not treated as a paperwork exercise.

Some supervisors require an ORSA-type report, but the scope, frequency and disclosure rules vary by country. Check the current local requirements rather than assuming one regime applies everywhere.

keyPoints: ERM manages risks across the whole insurer, not in separate silos.
Risk appetite states the risk the board will accept and is enforced through limits.
A risk register records each risk, its owner, impact, controls and actions.
Solvency ratio = eligible capital ÷ required capital.
Scenario-adjusted solvency ratio = (eligible capital − scenario loss) ÷ required capital.
ORSA-type assessments are insurer-owned and forward-looking, but their rules differ by country.

en.title: Actuarial mathematics for life insurance
en.short: Survival models, life tables, commutation functions, present values, net premiums and reserves, with a worked example.

sections.heading: Survival and life tables
sections.text: A survival model treats future lifetime T as a random variable. The survival function S(t) = P(T > t) gives the chance of living t more years. The force of mortality μ(x) is the instantaneous death rate at age x. A life table summarises a cohort: l_x is the number alive at exact age x, d_x = l_x − l_{x+1} is deaths before x+1, q_x = d_x ÷ l_x is the probability of dying in the year, and p_x = 1 − q_x is the probability of surviving it. Tables differ by country, sex and year.

sections.heading: Commutation and present values
sections.text: Commutation functions pack interest and mortality into tables. With v = 1 ÷ (1+i), D_x = v^x l_x, N_x = Σ D_{x+k}, C_x = v^{x+1} d_x and M_x = Σ C_{x+k}. For a whole life assurance paying 1 at the end of the year of death, A_x = M_x ÷ D_x. For a life annuity due paying 1 at the start of each year while alive, ä_x = N_x ÷ D_x. These present values use the same mortality basis and interest rate.

sections.heading: Net premiums and reserves
sections.text:
A net premium is the level annual premium whose present value equals the present value of benefits. For whole life assurance, P = A_x ÷ ä_x. The prospective policy reserve at duration t is V_t = A_{x+t} − P ä_{x+t}, the fund needed for future benefits less future premiums.

Example: l_50 = 1000, l_51 = 900, l_52 = 0, i = 10%, so v = 0.90909. Then q_50 = 100 ÷ 1000 = 0.1 and q_51 = 900 ÷ 900 = 1. A_50 = 0.90909 × 0.1 + 0.90909² × 0.9 × 1 = 0.83471. ä_50 = 1 + 0.90909 × 0.9 = 1.81818. P = 0.83471 ÷ 1.81818 = 0.45909. At duration 1, before the second premium, A_51 = 0.90909 and ä_51 = 1, so V_1 = 0.90909 − 0.45909 = 0.45 per unit of sum assured.

keyPoints: Survival function S(t) = P(T > t); q_x = d_x ÷ l_x and p_x = 1 − q_x.
Commutation functions: D_x = v^x l_x, N_x = Σ D_{x+k}, C_x = v^{x+1} d_x, M_x = Σ C_{x+k}.
Whole life assurance A_x = M_x ÷ D_x; life annuity due ä_x = N_x ÷ D_x.
Net premium P = A_x ÷ ä_x for a whole life policy with annual premiums.
Prospective reserve V_t = A_{x+t} − P ä_{x+t}.
Mortality tables and interest rates vary, so use the basis specified for the problem or valuation.

en.title: Reserving for general insurance claims
en.short: Covers outstanding claims, IBNR, chain-ladder and expected-loss methods, discounting and reserve uncertainty.

sections.heading: Claims reserves
sections.text: General insurers hold reserves for claims already incurred but not yet settled. Reported claims are estimated claim by claim and held as case reserves. Incurred but not reported (IBNR) reserves cover claims that have happened but are not yet known, plus later development on known claims. Case reserves plus IBNR make up the outstanding claims reserve. This is part of technical provisions, the total liabilities an insurer holds for unexpired risks and unpaid claims. Reserves are estimates, not exact debts. Actuaries and claims staff review them regularly.

sections.heading: Chain-ladder example
sections.text:
The chain-ladder method uses past cumulative paid claims to estimate how claims develop. For each development period, calculate a development factor: cumulative claims at the later period divided by the earlier period. Apply factors to the latest cumulative claims to reach an ultimate cost.

A made-up example, amounts in naira, cumulative paid claims:
2023: 1,000; 1,500; 1,800
2024: 1,200; 1,440
Development factor 1 to 2 = (1,500 + 1,440) ÷ (1,000 + 1,200) = 2,940 ÷ 2,200 = 1.336.
Development factor 2 to 3 = 1,800 ÷ 1,500 = 1.200.
Ultimate for 2024 = 1,440 × 1.200 = 1,728.
Reserve for 2024 = 1,728 − 1,440 = 288.

The method assumes development patterns are stable. Check the pattern and use other methods if it is not.

sections.heading: Expected loss, discounting, uncertainty
sections.text:
The expected-loss method applies an expected loss ratio to earned premium to estimate ultimate claims. It is useful when data are thin or for new lines. Expected ultimate claims = earned premium × expected loss ratio. Reserve = expected ultimate claims − paid claims. Subtracting reported outstanding claims as well gives the IBNR part.

Discounting reduces reserves to present value because claims are paid in future. The discount rate and rules vary by country and regulator, so check the current official source. Reserving uncertainty is high for long-tail liability, inflation, court awards and late reporting. Actuaries may add a risk margin and test scenarios. Reinsurance recoveries are shown separately and only if recoverable.

keyPoints: Case reserves cover reported claims, while IBNR covers claims incurred but not yet reported and later development; together they make up the outstanding claims reserve.
Chain-ladder development factor = cumulative claims at later development period ÷ cumulative claims at earlier period.
Ultimate claim = latest cumulative claim × product of remaining development factors.
Expected ultimate claims = earned premium × expected loss ratio; reserve = expected ultimate claims − paid claims; subtract reported outstanding claims as well for the IBNR part.
Discounting converts future claim payments to present value, and the rules vary by country.
Reserving uncertainty is highest for long-tail business, inflation and late reporting.

en.title: Insurance fraud
en.short: Types, red flags, investigation, controls, analytics and fair treatment in insurance fraud.

sections.heading: Types of fraud
sections.text: Insurance fraud is any deception by a person or firm to obtain money or benefit from an insurer or a customer, or to avoid a premium or obligation. Claims fraud includes invented, staged or exaggerated claims; a motor claim may inflate repair costs. Underwriting fraud is misrepresentation or non-disclosure at application. Premium fraud includes underpaying premiums or creating fictitious policies. Internal fraud involves staff or agents of the insurer. Provider fraud, such as health providers billing for services not given, is usually treated as external fraud. Criminal law and reporting duties vary by country.

sections.heading: Red flags and investigation
sections.text: Red flags are indicators, not proof: late notice, changed documents, inconsistent dates, repeated claims, refusal to explain, or a loss that fits a known pattern. Investigation should be proportionate: verify identity and documents, obtain statements, check databases and expert reports, and interview the claimant fairly. Keep records. Referral to police or a regulator depends on national law and the insurer’s duties; do not assume one country’s rules apply everywhere.

sections.heading: Controls and analytics
sections.text: Controls include identity and document checks at underwriting, claims triage (sorting claims by risk), separation of duties, supplier checks, staff training and confidential reporting channels. Data analytics compares claims with expected patterns using rules, anomaly detection and link analysis, which maps connections between people, vehicles or addresses. Models produce scores, not verdicts. False positives are common, so a high score should trigger review, not automatic rejection.

sections.heading: Fair treatment balance
sections.text: A concrete case: Ada files a genuine theft claim but her receipt is handwritten. A red flag stops automatic payment. The insurer should ask for other proof, explain the delay and decide promptly. Treating every claimant as a suspect harms trust and may breach fair treatment rules. Fraud control should be evidence-based, confidential and proportionate, with genuine claims paid without avoidable delay.

keyPoints: Insurance fraud includes claims, underwriting, premium and internal fraud.
Red flags are indicators, not proof of fraud.
Investigation must be proportionate, fair and documented.
Data analytics produces scores that need human review.
False positives are common, so automatic rejection is unsafe.
Criminal law and reporting duties vary by country.

en.title: Professional ethics and governance in insurance
en.short: Director duties, conduct standards, conflicts, whistleblowing, fair customer treatment and governance codes.

sections.heading: Governance and duties
sections.text: Corporate governance is the system by which the board directs and controls an insurer and is accountable to shareholders, policyholders and regulators. Directors must act in good faith in the company’s best interests, with care, skill and diligence. They must avoid or manage conflicts, disclose personal interests, and not misuse their position or inside information. Managers apply these standards, supervise staff and escalate breaches. Regulators also use fit and proper tests to check that directors and senior managers are honest, competent and financially sound. The detailed duties come from company law and regulator rules, so they differ by country.

sections.heading: Conduct and conflicts
sections.text: Conduct standards require honesty, integrity, competence, confidentiality and fair dealing. A conflict of interest arises when a personal interest, or a duty to another person, could affect professional judgement. Firms keep conflict registers, require disclosure, and ask affected people to step out of decisions. Whistleblowing is the reporting of wrongdoing, such as fraud or unsafe practice. A good policy gives staff an internal channel, allows confidential or anonymous reports, protects the reporter from retaliation and passes serious cases to the board or regulator.

sections.heading: Fair customer treatment
sections.text: Fair treatment of customers means clear product information, suitable advice, fair pricing, prompt claims payment and accessible complaints handling. It is a board responsibility, not only a marketing message. Managers should monitor outcomes, such as claim rejection rates and complaint patterns, and correct poor practice. Many regulators require firms to treat customers fairly, but the rules and names of the standards differ by country.

sections.heading: Case and codes
sections.text:
A made-up case: a claims manager at a Kenyan insurer finds that a director’s repair workshop has received inflated motor claims. She reports through the whistleblowing channel to the audit committee. The director discloses the interest, withdraws from related decisions, and the insurer retenders the contract.

Corporate governance codes set expectations for board independence, audit and risk committees, remuneration, disclosure and risk management. Many follow a comply or explain approach. Codes differ by country and by insurer type, so check the current local regulator and stock exchange requirements.

keyPoints: Directors must act in the insurer’s best interests, with care and skill, and manage conflicts.
Managers turn conduct standards into supervision, records and escalation.
Conflicts should be disclosed, recorded and avoided in decision making.
Whistleblowing channels must protect reporters from retaliation.
Fair treatment of customers covers information, advice, claims and complaints.
Governance codes differ by country and often work on comply or explain.

en.title: Advanced risk theory and ruin probability
en.short: Collective risk models, aggregate claims, adjustment coefficients and ruin probabilities.

sections.heading: Collective risk model
sections.text: The collective risk model treats total claims S over a period as a random sum: S = X1 + X2 + ... + XN. Here N is the number of claims (frequency) and each Xi is a claim amount (severity). N and the Xi are independent, and the Xi are identically distributed. Frequency is often Poisson, with mean and variance both λ. Poisson frequency with any severity distribution is called the compound Poisson model.

sections.heading: Aggregate claims
sections.text:
Two results follow. E(S) = E(N)E(X). Var(S) = E(N)Var(X) + Var(N)(E(X))². For compound Poisson, Var(N) = λ, so Var(S) = λE(X²).

Example: λ = 4 claims a year and every claim is exactly 500. Then E(S) = 4 × 500 = 2,000 and Var(S) = 4 × 500² = 1,000,000, so the standard deviation is 1,000.

sections.heading: Adjustment coefficient and ruin
sections.text: In the classical risk process the surplus is U(t) = u + ct − S(t), where u is the initial surplus and c the premium rate. Ruin means U(t) falls below zero at some time.
