The net profit condition c > λE(X) keeps the ruin probability below one. The adjustment coefficient R > 0 solves the Lundberg equation λ + cR = λE(e^{RX}). The Lundberg inequality then gives ψ(u) ≤ e^{−Ru}, and for large u the Cramér-Lundberg approximation is ψ(u) ≈ Ce^{−Ru}.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
Take Poisson claims with λ = 1, exponential severity with mean 1, and c = 1.5. The Lundberg equation is 1 + 1.5R = 1/(1 − R). Multiplying out gives (1 + 1.5R)(1 − R) = 1, so 0.5R − 1.5R² = 0 and R = 1/3. Check: 1 + 1.5(1/3) = 1.5 and 1/(1 − 1/3) = 1.5.

The safety loading is θ = c/(λE(X)) − 1 = 0.5. For exponential claims the exact ruin probability is ψ(u) = e^{−u/(1 + θ)} = e^{−2u/3}. At u = 3 this gives 0.135, below the Lundberg bound e^{−1} = 0.368.

keyPoints: Aggregate claims are a random sum of a random number of claim amounts.
E(S) = E(N)E(X) and Var(S) = E(N)Var(X) + Var(N)(E(X))².
For compound Poisson, Var(S) = λE(X²).
The net profit condition c > λE(X) is needed for ruin probability below one.
The adjustment coefficient R solves λ + cR = λE(e^{RX}).
The Lundberg inequality ψ(u) ≤ e^{−Ru} bounds the ruin probability.

en.title: Economics of insurance and information
en.short: Adverse selection, moral hazard, screening, signalling, contract design and why insurance is regulated.

sections.heading: Asymmetric information
sections.text: Insurance economics studies how insurers and buyers cope with hidden information. Asymmetric information means one side knows more than the other. Hidden type, the buyer’s risk level, causes adverse selection. Hidden action, the buyer’s care, causes moral hazard. Both are principal-agent problems: the insurer (principal) cannot fully observe the buyer (agent).

sections.heading: Adverse selection
sections.text: Adverse selection arises when high-risk buyers are more willing to buy at a given price. Suppose 100 buyers: 50 low-risk with expected claim 100 each, 50 high-risk with expected claim 500 each. Total expected claims = (50 × 100) + (50 × 500) = 30,000, so the average premium is 30,000 ÷ 100 = 300. Low-risk buyers may refuse 300 because their fair premium (expected claim) is 100. If they leave, the remaining average becomes 500, and the market can unravel.

sections.heading: Moral hazard and contracts
sections.text: Moral hazard arises after cover is bought: the insured may take less care because the insurer bears part of the loss. Optimal contract design trades off risk sharing against incentives. Deductibles, co-insurance, exclusions and no-claims discounts make the insured retain some loss. A deductible is the first part of a loss paid by the insured; co-insurance is a set share of the remaining loss. If a loss is 10,000, a deductible is 1,000 and co-insurance is 20%, the insurer pays (10,000 − 1,000) × 0.8 = 7,200. The insured bears 2,800.

sections.heading: Screening and regulation
sections.text: Screening means the insurer offers a menu of contracts, such as high deductible with low premium, so buyers reveal their type. Signalling means the informed buyer reveals information, for example through a medical report or voluntary audit. Regulation is justified because asymmetric information can cause market failure, insolvency and unfair treatment. Rules on disclosure, solvency and conduct vary by country, so check the local regime.

keyPoints: Hidden type causes adverse selection; hidden action causes moral hazard.
Average fair premium = total expected claims ÷ number of buyers.
Adverse selection can drive low-risk buyers out and make premiums rise.
Moral hazard is reduced by deductibles, co-insurance and other incentive devices.
Insurer payment = (loss − deductible) × (1 − co-insurance rate).
Screening uses contract menus, signalling uses credible disclosure, and regulation addresses market failure and consumer protection, with rules varying by country.

en.title: Research methods for insurance
en.short: Designing insurance research, choosing data and methods, sampling, validity, ethics and dissertation writing.

sections.heading: Research design
sections.text: Start with a question that insurance data can answer. A design is the plan linking question, evidence and argument. Exploratory work suits new areas; descriptive work measures frequency or severity; explanatory work tests relationships. State the unit of analysis, such as policy, claim, insurer or household, and the time period. A case study can combine interviews with documents. Keep the design feasible and ethical.

sections.heading: Data and sampling
sections.text: Insurance data include policy records, claims, premiums, exposure and complaints. Define each variable, check reconciliation and missing values, and pseudonymise personal data. Regulatory sources differ by country: for example, NAICOM in Nigeria, the PRA and FCA in the United Kingdom, and state insurance departments in the United States. They publish returns, accounts and codes. Sampling may be probability or non-probability. Rare claims need full data or oversampling. Expected claims = sample size × claim frequency. A sample of 500 motor policies at 5% claim frequency gives 25 claims, too few for stable severity estimates.

sections.heading: Methods and validity
sections.text: Quantitative methods include regression, survival analysis and comparisons of means; qualitative methods include interviews, focus groups and document analysis. Mixed methods can triangulate. Validity means the study measures what it claims: internal validity for causal claims, external validity for generalisation, construct validity for concepts. Watch selection, survivorship and reporting bias. Reliability means repeatable measurement. Pre-test instruments and keep an audit trail.

sections.heading: Ethics and writing
sections.text: Obtain ethics approval where required, informed consent, confidentiality and anonymity. Declare conflicts and follow the data protection law of the country. A dissertation has a clear question, literature review, method, results, discussion and limitations. Cite sources consistently, keep a data appendix and document cleaning steps so another researcher can follow them. Write limitations honestly.

keyPoints: A research design links the question, evidence and argument.
Define the unit of analysis and time period before collecting insurance data.
Regulatory sources differ by country, so name the regulator and check its current publications.
Expected claims in a sample = sample size × claim frequency.
Validity covers internal, external and construct validity; reliability concerns repeatability.
Ethics approval, consent, confidentiality and data protection law apply to insurance research.

en.title: Catastrophe risk, climate change and insurance
en.short: Covers catastrophe models, exposure, reinsurance, capital markets, parametric cover and climate gaps.

sections.heading: Catastrophe models
sections.text: Catastrophe models estimate the probability of losses from rare events. A model has four parts: hazard (the physical event), exposure (people, property and values at risk), vulnerability (the damage expected at each hazard intensity, often a damage ratio) and a financial module that turns damage into insured loss. Outputs include exceedance probability curves: the chance that a loss exceeds a given amount in a year. Models are uncertain, so insurers test assumptions against experience.

sections.heading: Exposure and vulnerability
sections.text: Exposure is what can be harmed; vulnerability is how easily it is harmed. A well-built hospital on high ground has lower vulnerability than a flimsy clinic on a flood plain. Climate change can raise hazard through more intense rainfall, heat and sea-level rise. Exposure also changes as populations grow and people move to cities and coasts. Where insurance is absent or too costly, losses fall on households, firms and governments. This is the protection gap. Its size and public schemes differ by country; check national sources.

sections.heading: Reinsurance and capital
sections.text: Insurers transfer catastrophe risk through reinsurance, such as catastrophe excess of loss, where the reinsurer pays losses above an agreed amount (the retention) up to a limit. Capital market solutions include catastrophe bonds and other insurance-linked securities: investors lend principal and lose some or all of it if a defined event occurs. Parametric insurance pays a fixed amount when a measured parameter, such as rainfall, passes a threshold. It settles quickly but carries basis risk: the payout may not match the actual loss.

sections.heading: Parametric example
sections.text: Example: a farm buys parametric flood cover. The trigger is 200 mm of rain in 72 hours; the payout is $50,000; the premium is $4,000. If rain reaches 210 mm, the farm receives $50,000 even if its loss is only $30,000. If rain is 190 mm and the loss is $60,000, there is no payout. Basis risk cuts both ways. Public schemes and insurance regulation vary by country.

keyPoints: Catastrophe models combine hazard, exposure, vulnerability and a financial module to estimate loss probabilities.
Exposure is what can be harmed; vulnerability is how easily it is harmed.
Reinsurance and insurance-linked securities transfer large catastrophe losses to reinsurers and investors.
Parametric insurance pays a fixed sum when a measured trigger is met, so basis risk is the gap between payout and actual loss.
The expected parametric payout equals the probability of the trigger multiplied by the fixed payout.
Protection gaps and public schemes vary by country, so check current national rules and sources.
